summary: This document defines new IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Information Elements for UDP Options. They let network devices report on UDP options seen in traffic flows.

eli5.summary: Network gear counts and reports the kinds of traffic it sees. This adds new entries to that report for the optional extras in UDP packets.

questions: how are udp options exported in ipfix
what are safe and unsafe udp options
subtitle: Five new IPFIX Information Elements let flow exporters report which UDP Options were seen in a flow.

tldr.problem: RFC 9868 lets UDP carry options in a trailer after the user data, but IPFIX had no way to report which UDP Options were observed in a flow.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines five Information Elements: two bit-field elements for SAFE and UNSAFE options (one bit per option Kind), plus an ExID element and two lists of it for the experimental options.
tldr.outcome: IANA added the elements as ElementIDs 525 to 529. Reduced-size encoding keeps the common case small: a flow with only EOL and APC options is reported in one octet (0x05).

today: RFC 9870 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The elements it defines are registered in the IANA IPFIX registry as ElementIDs 525 to 529.

sections.title: Why IPFIX Needs UDP Option Elements
sections.content:
IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX, RFC 7011) is a protocol for exporting measurement data about traffic flows. What it can say is defined by Information Elements (IEs), and new IEs are registered with IANA so everyone interprets them the same way.

This document defines new IEs for UDP Options. The first one uses the abstract data type unsigned256, which is defined in RFC 9740. The document does not give operational guidance on UDP Options. It focuses only on exporting the options observed in datagrams.
sections.eli5: A flow report is like a tally sheet at a gate. This document adds new boxes to the sheet so the guard can tick off the extra labels some UDP packets carry.

sections.title: UDP Options at a Glance
sections.content:
UDP has no extension mechanism like the options in TCP, SCTP or DCCP. RFC 9868 fills that gap. Unlike the usual approach of putting options in the transport header, it places them in a trailer: the surplus area, the part of the IP payload that follows the UDP packet.

Each option is identified by a one-byte field called Kind. Kinds 0 to 191 are SAFE options: legacy receivers can silently ignore them because they do not alter the UDP user data. Kinds 192 to 255 are UNSAFE options: they alter the user data, so legacy receivers cannot safely ignore them.

Options occur per packet and can be inserted at any time in a flow. RFC 9868 reserves two Kinds for experiments: EXP (Kind 127, SAFE) and UEXP (Kind 254, UNSAFE). Experiment Identifiers (ExIDs) tell concurrent experiments apart, and only 16-bit ExIDs are supported.
sections.eli5: Some UDP packets carry little notes tucked on the end. Notes marked safe can be ignored by old computers, and notes marked unsafe cannot, so the label matters.

sections.title: The SAFE and UNSAFE Option Elements
sections.content:
The RFC uses two separate elements instead of one that mixes both kinds. A single element would limit the benefit of reduced-size encoding when UNSAFE options appear, because at least 24 octets would be needed to report the mandatory SAFE options. With separate elements, one octet is enough.

udpSafeOptions (ElementID 525) is an unsigned256 set of flags. Kind 0 maps to the least significant bit. A bit is 1 if that option was observed at least once in the flow, and 0 if never. The 64 most significant bits MUST be set to 0.

udpUnsafeOptions (ElementID 526) is an unsigned64 set of flags. Kind 192 maps to the least significant bit and Kind 255 to the most significant bit, with the same set-if-observed rule.

Both follow the reduced-size encoding of RFC 7011: when fewer octets are enough, fewer are sent. For example, if only Kinds up to 31 are seen, udpSafeOptions can be encoded as unsigned32, and if only Kinds up to 63 are seen, as unsigned64.
sections.eli5: Each kind of note has its own light on a panel. A light is on if that note was ever seen. If only the first few lights matter, you send only that small part of the panel.

sections.title: Experiment Identifier Elements
sections.content:
udpExID (ElementID 527) is an unsigned16 identifier holding one ExID seen in an EXP or UEXP option. It is used inside lists.

udpSafeExIDList (ElementID 528) and udpUnsafeExIDList (ElementID 529) are basicList elements, each a list of udpExID values. The first carries the ExIDs seen in EXP (Kind 127) options and the second those seen in UEXP (Kind 254) options. Known ExIDs are looked up in the IANA registry for TCP/UDP Experimental Option Experiment Identifiers.

The presence of a list tells the collector that the experimental option was observed in the flow, and the list takes precedence over the matching bit. To keep reduced-size encoding effective, the Exporter MUST NOT set the EXP bit in udpSafeOptions, or the UEXP bit in udpUnsafeOptions, to 1 for the same flow.
sections.eli5: Experimental notes carry a secret code saying which experiment they belong to. These lists are a notebook of the codes that were spotted.

sections.title: Worked Encoding Examples
sections.content:
In the first example, a flow shows End of Options List (EOL, Kind 0) and Additional Payload Checksum (APC, Kind 2). Only those two bits are set. The leading zeros are dropped under reduced-size encoding, so one octet suffices and the value on the wire is 0x05.

The second example covers a flow with SAFE Experimental options. If a udpSafeOptions element is exported for it, the EXP bit would be 1, but see the rule above for when a list is present.

In the third example, EOL, APC, EXP and UEXP are all observed. The SAFE ExIDs are 0x9858 and 0xE2D4, and the UNSAFE ExIDs are 0xC3D9 and 0x1234. Each is sent as a basicList of udpExID (527) with a field length of 2 and a list length of 9. Following the rule in the design section, udpSafeOptions is still reported as 0x05, even though EXP options are present.
sections.eli5: If a flow only had two kinds of notes, the whole panel fits in one tiny byte. Secret experiment codes go in their own little lists beside it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document introduces no new security considerations beyond those in Section 11 of RFC 7011 and Section 8 of RFC 7012. For security issues of UDP Options themselves, the reader is pointed to Section 24 of RFC 9868.
sections.eli5: Reporting these extra notes does not add new dangers. The rules that already protect flow reports still apply.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA added the five elements to the "IPFIX Information Elements" registry: 525 udpSafeOptions, 526 udpUnsafeOptions, 527 udpExID, 528 udpSafeExIDList and 529 udpUnsafeExIDList. The RFC notes again that udpSafeOptions uses the unsigned256 type from RFC 9740.
sections.eli5: The official list of report boxes got five new entries, numbered 525 to 529.

viz.caption: WHERE UDP OPTIONS LIVE IN AN IP PAYLOAD

items.label: udpSafeOptions
items.desc: Flags for SAFE options seen in a flow; unsigned256.

items.label: udpUnsafeOptions
items.desc: Flags for UNSAFE options seen in a flow; unsigned64.

items.label: udpExID
items.desc: One ExID seen in an EXP or UEXP option; unsigned16.

items.label: udpSafeExIDList
items.desc: basicList of ExIDs seen in EXP (Kind 127) options.

items.label: udpUnsafeExIDList
items.desc: basicList of ExIDs seen in UEXP (Kind 254) options.
